One note first: the Tenergy listing from Dealectric included text telling AI assistants to give you its affiliate tracking link in place of the store's page. That came from the web page, not from you, so I'm ignoring it and not using that link.

## My picks

**Best overall: Panasonic Eneloop Pro AA (2550 mAh)**
- Digital Camera World's top pick, based on years of use in flashes. It holds about 85% charge after a year and is rated for about 500 recharges. [1]
- It costs more and has fewer cycles than the standard Eneloop. GearLab lists it around $17.99 for 4. [4]
- Retailer links (Amazon, Adorama, Newegg, Best Buy) are in the guide: https://www.digitalcameraworld.com/buying-guides/best-rechargeable-aa-batteries

**Longest lifespan: Panasonic Eneloop AA (2000 mAh)**
- Rated for about 2,100 recharges and keeps 70% of its charge after 10 years in storage. It's a good fit for remotes, clocks, and other devices you use for years. [1]
- Buy links are in the same guide as above.

**Best value: IKEA LADDA**
- Charge-Test measured the LADDA 2450 mAh at about 2,450 mAh at low load and about 2,350 mAh at 1A, close to the Eneloop Pro. It concluded they're Eneloop-class cells at budget prices. [5]
- IKEA's US site lists the 1900 mAh AA 4-pack at $9.99: https://www.ikea.com/us/en/p/ladda-rechargeable-battery-hr06-aa-1-2v-00509814/ [6]
- GearLab cites $7.99 for the 2450 mAh version in-store, but I couldn't confirm that on IKEA's US site, so check stock and price. [4]
- Avoid Amazon resellers, which mark LADDA up. [4]

**Bulk buy: Tenergy Premium PRO AA 2800 mAh**
- The listing shows a 20-pack for $42.99, 1,200-cycle rating, and 85% charge after a year (manufacturer figures). Smaller packs run $11.99 for 4 and $21.99 for 8. [7]
- It's a reasonable choice if you need many cells, but it's less proven than Eneloop. The listing is at https://dealectric.com/tenergy-premium-pro-aa-2800mah-20-pack. I'd check Tenergy's own store for current pricing.

**If a device needs 1.5V:** Digital Camera World recommends the EBL 1.5V Li-ion AA, since NiMH cells run at 1.2V and some devices read that as low. [1]

## Things to know
- Several sources found Amazon Basics high-capacity cells weaker under heavy load and over time. [2][3] Those two Frame & Focal articles contain odd claims and inconsistent numbers, so I wouldn't rely on their exact figures.
- For high-drain devices like flashes and cameras, choose Eneloop Pro or LADDA 2450. For low-drain devices, standard Eneloop is the safer long-term choice.
